summary: The session agent proposed delegation, an API/MCP adapter, native ACP integration, and scheduled monitoring. It did not verify an existing connector.
speaker: FairyStack session agent
source_quote:
Yes—Hermes could interface with FairyStack in several useful ways. The building blocks exist, though I haven’t verified a ready-made Hermes–FairyStack connector.

| Approach | What it would let you do | Work required |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Hermes delegates to FairyStack** | Ask Hermes to build or fix an app; FairyStack runs the coding session and deployment. | A small API connector. |
| **Hermes uses FairyStack tools** | Let Hermes inspect apps and perform authorized management actions itself. | An MCP adapter around FairyStack’s APIs, plus execution access for code changes. |
| **Hermes runs inside FairyStack** | Choose Hermes as the agent behind a FairyStack conversation, retaining its memory and skills. | A deeper runtime integration using ACP. |
| **Hermes monitors your apps** | Run scheduled checks and request a FairyStack repair session when needed. | Scheduled Hermes work plus the API connector. |

**The quickest useful starting point is delegation.** FairyStack already documents an integration API for creating agent sessions, checking their status, and stopping them. Hermes could submit “fix this app,” retain the returned session ID, and follow progress. A scoped integration key limits it to sessions it starts; the API includes concurrency limits and failure controls. It does **not** grant transcript access or steering, so returning detailed results to Hermes would need an explicit result channel. [FairyStack API guide](https://multi.fairystack.com/agent-guide.md)

**MCP is the natural option for giving Hermes tools.** Hermes supports local and remote MCP servers, automatic tool discovery, and tool filtering. We could expose a small FairyStack toolset—such as app inventory and session start/status/stop—through an adapter. The adapter would handle authentication and timeouts; deployment would still use FairyStack’s supported deployment boundary. [Hermes MCP documentation](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/mcp)

**ACP is the interesting option if you want Hermes here in the chat.** Hermes can run as an ACP server with `hermes acp`, exposing messages, tool activity, diffs, permission requests, and streamed responses while keeping its existing configuration, memory, and skills. FairyStack would need a host adapter that connects those events to its conversations, credentials, cancellation, and completion tracking. This is a proposed integration, not a switch I found already available. [Hermes ACP documentation](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/acp)

My recommendation: start with **Hermes as your persistent personal agent and FairyStack as its app-building service**. That gives you a useful connection with relatively little integration work. If your main goal is to talk to Hermes directly through FairyStack’s interface, prioritize ACP instead.

summary: The session agent proposed an ACP runtime, ownership boundaries, project-scoped profiles, and restart/resume testing. No final architecture agreement was recorded.
speaker: FairyStack session agent
source_quote:
Got it—you’re building the FairyStack side, and we’re figuring out the design. **I’d make Hermes a runtime behind FairyStack’s existing conversation interface**, with ACP as the first transport to evaluate. Hermes explicitly supports another application owning conversation transport while it retains its memory, skills, tools, and provider configuration. [Hermes ACP docs](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/acp)

The ownership split I’d propose:

| FairyStack owns | Hermes owns |
| --- | --- |
| Human identity, room membership, who may address the agent | Agent reasoning and tool execution |
| Visible conversations and durable execution records | Runtime conversation context and compaction |
| Workspace allocation, scoped credentials, deployment boundaries | Skills and persistent agent memory |
| Starting, stopping, deadlines, and reporting failures | Model/provider interaction |

A normal interaction would work like this:

1. The user selects Hermes for a FairyStack conversation.
2. FairyStack starts or reconnects to a Hermes worker on the execution machine, with the intended workspace and isolated profile.
3. FairyStack sends the user’s message through ACP and maps returned text, tool activity, and permission requests into its existing UI.
4. FairyStack records completion or failure. On Stop, it requests cancellation and enforces a deadline if the worker fails to stop.

**The most consequential choice is memory scope.** Should this feel like *your one persistent Hermes*, present across conversations, or a separate Hermes for each project? I’d start with one profile per owner and project, with separate runtime sessions per conversation. That preserves continuity without silently mixing unrelated projects or different people’s private context. A shared room’s access to that profile should be explicit.

For the first implementation, I’d keep scheduling under FairyStack’s control and leave Hermes’s messaging gateway out of the path. Otherwise two systems could independently initiate work or deliver replies. Hermes’s default ACP toolset already excludes messaging delivery and cron management. [ACP toolset](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/acp)

The first useful prototype is one conversation with streaming, tool activity, Stop, and reconnect after a worker restart. **Verify resume semantics before building around them**: mapping a FairyStack conversation to a Hermes session ID is straightforward; proving that a restart resumes correctly without replaying side effects is the important part. MCP can then supply FairyStack-specific tools alongside ACP’s conversation transport.

summary: The session agent proposed isolated unattended synchronization through polling or webhooks. It distinguished pulling swarm-forensics from deploying Swarm Touchpoint and said recurring sync was not configured.
speaker: FairyStack session agent
source_quote:
Yes. There are two useful levels:

- **Before each task:** fetch GitHub changes, then fast-forward a clean local `main`. I already do this. The checkout is currently up to date.
- **While nobody is working:** a scheduled check or GitHub webhook can detect new commits and trigger synchronization.

For unattended sync, I’d use a separate checkout so updates cannot change files underneath an active agent. It would fetch the new revision, run tests and lint, and report success or failure. A working checkout with uncommitted changes or diverging commits would be left intact.

**Pulling code and deploying the app are separate steps.** The live Swarm Touchpoint app also has a separate repository; changes to `swarm-forensics` won’t automatically update it.

Unattended synchronization isn’t configured yet. Scheduled polling is possible with our current access; configuring a repository webhook may require additional GitHub permissions.
